Since communication involves letters and symbols as well as numbers there are two alphanumeric codes often used.
ASCII stands for the American Standard Code for Information Interchange. This is a partial listing of characters and commands represented by ASCII codes.
The ASCII code uses a 011 prefix plus the BCD (8421) code for decimal digits. Other prefixes and code combinations are used for letters, symbols, and commands.
For example, the letter A uses ASCII code 1000001 and an asterisk is 0101010.
Now, let's look at the EBCDIC code.........................
EBCDIC stands for Extended Binary-Coded Decimal Interchange Code. This is a partial listing of characters and commands represented by EBCDIC codes.
The EBCDIC code uses a 1111 prefix plus the BCD (8421) code for decimal digits. Other prefixes and code combinations are used for letters, symbols, and commands.

Definition
The Gray code is another code often used in digital electronic applications.
The bits in the Gray code do not carry a weighted value like the BCD code so we cannot associate position with a specific value.
The Gray code is significant because only one bit changes as we move from one code number to the next.
For example, only one bit changes as the Gray code 0001 changes to 0011 when we move from a decimal 1 to a decimal 2. Two bits must change as the BCD code 0001 changes to 0010.

Let's learn about one of the most commonly used codes called the binary coded decimal (BCD) code.
Binary numbers are easily converted to decimal equivalents but we usually cannot identify the decimal value by simply looking at the binary number.
The BCD code uses a set of four binary digits (bits) to represent each decimal digit.
The BCD code represents each decimal digit by a set of four bits.
Each bit carries a weighted value determined by its position.
For example, a 1 in the position 0010 has a value of 2 while a 1 in the position 1000 has a value of 8.
The decimal equivalents are found by adding the weights of the bit positions. A BCD code of 1001 is 8 + 1 which equals 9.
To determine the decimal equivalent of a binary number in BCD code we separate the number into sets of four bits and write the decimal number represented by each set.
A BCD code of 0001 is a decimal 1, 0000 BCD is a decimal 0 and 0011 BCD is a decimal 3.
We simply reverse the process in order to convert a decimal number to BCD code.
Each digit of the decimal number is written in its four bit BCD code.
